report:
### Evidence Summary: Dark Chocolate and Stroke Risk

**Conclusion:** Scientific evidence suggests that moderate intake of dark chocolate and cocoa flavanols is **associated with a reduced risk of stroke**, though definitive proof of direct causality from dark chocolate products remains limited.

#### Key Findings
* **Observational Studies:** Meta-analyses of large prospective cohort studies show that moderate chocolate consumption is associated with a 10% to 20% lower relative risk of stroke and overall cardiovascular events ([Neurology](https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0b013e31826aacfa); [Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-019-01914-9)).
* **Biological Mechanisms:** Dark chocolate contains high concentrations of cocoa flavanols (polyphenols). Clinical trials demonstrate that these compounds improve nitric oxide production, enhance endothelial blood vessel function, reduce platelet aggregation, and slightly lower blood pressure—key factors in stroke prevention ([AJCN](https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)02692-8/fulltext)).
* **Limitations:** Researchers emphasize that observational data carry a risk of residual confounding (e.g., chocolate consumers may share other healthy lifestyle habits) ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-019-01914-9)). Furthermore, many dark chocolate products contain high levels of added sugar, saturated fat, and calories, which can cause weight gain and counter vascular benefits if eaten in excess ([American Heart Association](https://www.heart.org/en/news/2019/02/12/are-there-health-benefits-from-chocolate)).

In summary, while dark chocolate rich in cocoa flavanols offers vascular benefits, it should be consumed in moderation as part of a balanced diet.
